title: About
text:
Here I post some interesting PHREEQC use cases that I came across. I minimize use of AI for text writing, so no long explanations. I mostly use python to generate and run PHREEQC scripts. Occasionally, I would use FiPy coupled with PHREEQC. My OS is linux and code setup is optimized for that. If you cannot figure out how to use my codes on your OS, there is high chance you do not need it, and there is a simpler solution for your problem.
If you have questions feel free to contact me via LinkedIn.

title: Add DUMP functionality to phreeqpy
text:
According to the manual phreeqpy exposes all available methods of PHREEQC module. However, method GET_DUMP_STRING_LINES and DUMP related methods are not available. But we know that DUMP instructions are very useful for exporting the exact state of a cell or exchanger, for example when computing transport outside of PHREEQC. Perhaps, I misread phreeqpy the documentation. Below is a vibe-coded modification of phreeqpy that correctly exposes methods related to DUMP instruction. I hardly take any credit here as the code was fully produced by ChatGPT.
The usage is explained below as well. A word of caution. Sometimes, it cases ipython kernel crash when you try accessing the DUMP string(s). This most likely means you forgot to put an END at the end of a simulation.
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
Overlay for phreeqpy.iphreeqc.phreeqc_dll that adds complete DUMP controls:
- GetDumpFileOn / SetDumpFileOn
- GetDumpStringOn / SetDumpStringOn
- GetDumpStringLineCount / GetDumpStringLine

Usage (example):
    from iphreeqc_dump_overlay import IPhreeqc
    phc = IPhreeqc()  # or IPhreeqc(dll_path=".../libiphreeqc-*.so|dll|dylib")
    phc.load_database("/path/to/phreeqc.dat")
    phc.set_dump_file_on(False)       # disable writing to file
    phc.set_dump_string_on(True)      # capture DUMP into string buffer
    phc.run_string("SOLUTION 1; temp 25; pH 7; DUMP; -all; END")
    print(phc.get_dump_string())      # entire dump as one string

Run module as a script for a quick self-test:
    python -m iphreeqc_dump_overlay --db /full/path/to/phreeqc.dat
"""

import ctypes
import os
import sys
from ctypes import c_int, c_char_p

# --- import base wrapper
from phreeqpy.iphreeqc.phreeqc_dll import IPhreeqc as _BaseIPhreeqc  # noqa: E402


def _default_lib_path_from_package():
    """
    Reproduce phreeqpy's platform-specific library selection,
    but resolve path relative to the phreeqpy.iphreeqc package.
    """
    import phreeqpy.iphreeqc as iph_pkg
    base = os.path.dirname(iph_pkg.__file__)
    if sys.platform == "win32":
        dll_name = "phreeqc3/IPhreeqc-3.7.3.dll"
    elif sys.platform.startswith("linux"):
        dll_name = "phreeqc3/libiphreeqc-3.7.3.so"
    elif sys.platform == "darwin":
        machine = os.uname()[-1]
        if machine == "x86_64":
            dll_name = "phreeqc3/libiphreeqc-3.7.3.dylib"
        elif machine == "arm64":
            dll_name = "phreeqc3/libiphreeqc-3.7.3-m1.dylib"
        else:
            raise NotImplementedError(f"Unsupported macOS arch: {machine}")
    else:
        raise NotImplementedError(f"Unsupported platform: {sys.platform}")
    return os.path.join(base, dll_name)


class IPhreeqc(_BaseIPhreeqc):
    """
    Subclass that adds DUMP-related method bindings via ctypes.

    Notes on binding:
    - C API returns/accepts int for on/off switches; we convert to bool in Python.
    - Line accessors return const char*; ctypes maps that as c_char_p.
    """

    def __init__(self, dll_path=None):
        # Initialize base class (loads the library for its own symbols)
        super().__init__(dll_path=dll_path)

        # We bind needed symbols ourselves, using the same library file path
        # resolution logic as phreeqpy, unless caller provided dll_path.
        if dll_path is None:
            dll_path = _default_lib_path_from_package()

        lib = ctypes.cdll.LoadLibrary(dll_path)

        # ---- Dump file switch
        self._get_dump_file_on = lib.GetDumpFileOn
        self._get_dump_file_on.argtypes = [c_int]
        self._get_dump_file_on.restype = c_int

        self._set_dump_file_on = lib.SetDumpFileOn
        self._set_dump_file_on.argtypes = [c_int, c_int]
        self._set_dump_file_on.restype = c_int

        # ---- Dump string switch
        self._get_dump_string_on = lib.GetDumpStringOn
        self._get_dump_string_on.argtypes = [c_int]
        self._get_dump_string_on.restype = c_int

        self._set_dump_string_on = lib.SetDumpStringOn
        self._set_dump_string_on.argtypes = [c_int, c_int]
        self._set_dump_string_on.restype = c_int

        # ---- Dump string accessors
        self._get_dump_string_line_count = lib.GetDumpStringLineCount
        self._get_dump_string_line_count.argtypes = [c_int]
        self._get_dump_string_line_count.restype = c_int

        self._get_dump_string_line = lib.GetDumpStringLine
        self._get_dump_string_line.argtypes = [c_int, c_int]
        self._get_dump_string_line.restype = c_char_p

    # ---------------------------
    # Python-friendly wrappers
    # ---------------------------

    # File on/off (writes to dump file on disk)
    def get_dump_file_on(self) -> bool:
        """True if writing to the DUMP file is enabled."""
        return bool(self._get_dump_file_on(self.id_))

    def set_dump_file_on(self, on: bool = True):
        """Enable/disable writing to the DUMP file."""
        err = self._set_dump_file_on(self.id_, 1 if on else 0)
        if err < 0:
            self.raise_ipq_error(err)

    # String on/off (captures DUMP into an internal string buffer)
    def get_dump_string_on(self) -> bool:
        """True if capturing DUMP to an internal string buffer is enabled."""
        return bool(self._get_dump_string_on(self.id_))

    def set_dump_string_on(self, on: bool = True):
        """Enable/disable capturing DUMP into a string buffer."""
        err = self._set_dump_string_on(self.id_, 1 if on else 0)
        if err < 0:
            self.raise_ipq_error(err)

    # Access DUMP string contents
    def get_dump_string_line_count(self) -> int:
        """Number of lines currently stored in the DUMP string buffer."""
        return int(self._get_dump_string_line_count(self.id_))

    def get_dump_string_line(self, n: int) -> str:
        """Return one line (0-based) from the DUMP string buffer."""
        b = self._get_dump_string_line(self.id_, int(n))
        return "" if not b else b.decode("utf-8")

    def get_dump_string_lines(self) -> list[str]:
        """Return the entire DUMP buffer as a list of lines."""
        cnt = self.get_dump_string_line_count()
        return [self.get_dump_string_line(i) for i in range(cnt)]

    def get_dump_string(self) -> str:
        """Return the entire DUMP buffer as a single string."""
        return "\n".join(self.get_dump_string_lines())

    # ---------------------------
    # Quick self-test / debug aid
    # ---------------------------

    def _self_test_dump(self, database_path: str) -> None:
        """
        Minimal end-to-end test:
        - loads database
        - enables string capture
        - runs a tiny input with DUMP
        - checks that DUMP buffer contains content
        """
        if not os.path.exists(database_path):
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Database not found: {database_path}")

        # Ensure clean state
        self.set_dump_file_on(False)
        self.set_dump_string_on(False)

        # Load DB
        self.load_database(database_path)
        if self.phc_database_error_count != 0:
            raise RuntimeError("Database load reported errors:\n" + self.get_error_string())

        # Turn on DUMP-to-string capture
        self.set_dump_string_on(True)

        # Simple input that triggers a DUMP block
        inp = (
            "SOLUTION 1\n"
            "    temp 25\n"
            "    pH 7 charge\n"
            "DUMP\n"
            "    -all\n"
            "END\n"
        )
        self.run_string(inp)

        # Validate that we got something back
        line_count = self.get_dump_string_line_count()
        assert line_count >= 1, "DUMP buffer is empty; expected at least one line."
        # Spot-check a few first lines for plausibility (not strict, just helpful)
        first = self.get_dump_string_line(0)
        if not isinstance(first, str):
            raise AssertionError("DUMP line is not a string")
        # Optional: print a short preview
        preview = "\n".join(self.get_dump_string_lines()[:5])
        print("[iphreeqc_dump_overlay] DUMP preview (first lines):\n", preview)


# ---------------------------
# CLI for quick validation
# ---------------------------

def _main():
    import argparse

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Quick DUMP overlay self-test.")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--db",
        required=True,
        help="Full path to phreeqc.dat (or another PHREEQC database).",
    )
    parser.add_argument(
        "--dll",
        default=None,
        help="Optional full path to libiphreeqc shared library; "
             "if omitted, platform default from phreeqpy package is used.",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    iph = IPhreeqc(dll_path=args.dll)
    iph._self_test_dump(args.db)
    print("[iphreeqc_dump_overlay] OK")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()

title: Use of Phreeqcpy package in python
text:
import phreeqpy.iphreeqc.phreeqc_dll as phreeqc_mod
import pandas as pd


#%% PHREEQC setup

phc1 = phreeqc_mod.IPhreeqc('/home/yutkinm/IPHREEQC/lib/libiphreeqc.so')
db_path = "/home/yutkinm/IPHREEQC/share/doc/iphreeqc/database/phreeqc.dat"
phc1.load_database(db_path)

def get_so(iph):
    out = iph.get_selected_output_array()
    return pd.DataFrame(out[1:], columns=out[0])

#%%

pc_input = """

SELECTED_OUTPUT 1
reset true

SOLUTION 1
END
"""

phc1.run_string(pc_input)

output = get_so(phc1)

print(output)

title: Kinetics of 1:1 Ion Exchange
text:
Short theory
Let’s start by considering the following ion exchange equation: \[
\ce{>S-Na + Li+ <-->[K_{ex}] >S-Li + Na+}
\]
for this equation \(K_{\text{ex}} = [S_{\ce{Li}}][C_{\ce{Na+}}] / [S_{\ce{Na}}][C_{\ce{Li+}}]\), where \(S\) denotes surface concentrations in mol/kgw and \(C\) denotes bulk concentrations in mol/kgw. In such formulation equilibrium constant is dimensionless, which is convenient.
To formulate Basic program in PHREEQC for kinetics we seek an expression of the form: \(\text{rate} = dS_{\ce{Na}}/dt = k_r (K^{\prime} C_{\ce{Na+}} - S_{\ce{Na}})\), where \(K^{\prime}\) is not necessarily equal to \(K_{\text{ex}}\), and \(k_r\) is a rate constant in m/s. We also note that lithium exchange rate is equal and opposite in sign. We now consider three ways of obtaining such an expression.


1. Exponential decay
We start with exponential decay because it is the easiest way and is described in hydrochemistry.eu, and we also get to pick sign convention in PHREEQC for kinetics expressions.
In this formulation \(\text{rate} = k_r (S^e_{\ce{Na}} - S_{\ce{Na}})\). Once the equilibrium state is known, computation of the rate is straight forward.
Here is a simple example slightly modified from hydrochemistry.eu:
SELECTED_OUTPUT 1
-reset true
-kinetic_reactants kin_exch_na kin_exch_li

RATES
 kin_exch_na
# kinetic exchange: d(q_Na)/dt = k * (q_Na_eq - q_Na)
# q_Na_eq is equilibrium exchangeable Na 
-start
 10 q_Na_eq = {S_Na_eq}
 20 q_Na = m
 30 dq_Na = 100 * (q_Na_eq - q_Na) * time
 40 save -dq_Na
-end

 kin_exch_li
# kinetic exchange: d(q_K)/dt = k * (q_K_eq - q_K)
-start
 10 q_Li_eq = {S_Li_eq}
 20 q_Li = m
 30 dq_Li = 100 * (q_Li_eq - q_Li) * time
 40 save -dq_Li
-end

KINETICS 1
 kin_exch_na;  -formula Na 1.0
 m0 0.55e-3
 
 kin_exch_li;  -formula Li 1.0
 m0 0.55e-3
Note the sign convention when saving moles in RATE and in formula for KINETICS.


2. Small deviation from a reference equilibrium state
If we now incorporate mass and charge balance in the equilibrium exchange constant expression, such that \(CEC = S_{\ce{Na}} + S_{\ce{Li}}\) and \(C_{\ce{Cl-}} = C_{\ce{Na+}} + C_{\ce{Li+}}\), we obtain an expression of \([S_\ce{Li}(Li)]\) (yes, I switched to lithium here, but it does not matter) that we hope to have in the form suitable for our RATES law.
\[
[S_\ce{Li}(Li)] = \cfrac{K_{\text{ex}}C_{\ce{Li+}} CEC}{C_{\ce{Cl-}} + (K_{\text{ex}} - 1)C_{\ce{Li+}}}
\]
The slope of the tangent at a reference state (0) is given by \(dS/dt = K C_{\ce{Cl-}}CEC / (C_{\ce{Cl-}} + (K - 1)C_{\ce{Li_0}})^2 \equiv K^{\prime}\). Small deviations from the reference state are linear such that \(\Delta S_{\ce{Li}} \approx K^{\prime}\Delta C_{\ce{Li+}}\). We thus can write RATES Basic program.
RATES
Li_Na_lin_exch
-start
  10 CEC_tot   = {CEC}
  20 logK_LiX  = {log_KLi}
  30 Li0       = {Li_ref}
  40 S_Li0     = {s_Li_ref}
  50 k_r       = {k_r}
  60 S_Li = m
  70 Li         = MOL("Li+")
  80 Cl_tot     = TOT("Cl")
  90 K_GT       = 10^logK_LiX
 100 denom      = Cl_tot + (K_GT - 1.0)*Li0
 110 IF (denom <= 0) THEN denom = 1E-30
 120 K_loc  = K_GT * CEC_tot * Cl_tot / (denom * denom)
 130 dLi   = Li   - Li0
 140 dS_Li = S_Li - S_Li0
 150 dS_Li_eq = K_loc * dLi
 160 rate_S_Li = k_r * (dS_Li_eq - dS_Li)
 170 moles = rate_S_Li * TIME
 180 SAVE -moles
-end

KINETICS 1
Li_Na_lin_exch
 -formula Li+ 1 Na+ -1   
 -m      {s_Li_init}  
There are two important caveats: 1) this rate law is valid only at small deviations from the reference state; 2) this rate law assumes that we are at the same adsorption isotherm (i.e. \(C_{\ce{Cl-}}\) is constant and the same at the reference state and the new state).
Also, note that the always dimensionless equilibrium exchange constant used by PHREEQC (i.e. Gaines-Thomas convention) in the linear case equal to the equilibrium exchange constant I used. This will not be the case for a non-linear ion exchange, which is considered (here).
While such a rate is rather limited, it is easy and fast to compute (i.e. it has closed form solution or would require a simple and efficient itegrator) and thus lookup tables can be pre-generated for it easily when solving chemistry on large grids. The same conclusion applies to the first considered rate law.


3. Full kinetic expression
Finally, we could use full rate expression obtained directly from the equilibrium exchange constant. Again we seek an expression of the form \(\text{rate} = dS_{\ce{Li}}/dt = k_r (K^{\prime} C_{\ce{Li+}} - S_{\ce{Li}})\). From the equilibrium constant we obtain:
\[
K^{\prime} = \cfrac{K_{\text{ex}} CEC}{(C_{\ce{Cl-}} + (K_{\text{ex}} - 1)C_{\ce{Li+}})}
\]
Then the RATES program is as follows.
SELECTED_OUTPUT 1
-reset true
-kinetic_reactants Li_Na_lin_exch 

RATES
Li_Na_lin_exch
-start
 10 CEC = {CEC}
 20 K = {10**log_KLi}
 140 K_prime = K * CEC/(MOL("Cl-") + (K-1)*(MOL("Cl-") - MOL("Na+")))
 150 driver = (K_prime * MOL("Li+") - m)
 160 rate = {k_r} * driver
 170 moles = rate * TIME
 180 save -moles
-end

KINETICS 1
Li_Na_lin_exch
 -formula Li+ 1 Na+ -1   
 -m      {s_Li_init}  
 -cvode true
The important caveat here is that we used equilibrium constant expression to obtain expression for \(K^{\prime}\), but we use actual ionic concentrations, not equilibrium. In other words, numerically we are not integrating towards a constant or linear target, we are integrating toward a moving target, which is dependent on state.


Comparison of the three cases
So, now it would make sense to compare performance of these rate laws using PHREEQC. However, there is one complication. PHREEQC actually uses activities instead of concentrations and above rate expressions are based on charge balance tied to \(C_{\ce{Cl-}}\) molar concentration. Thus, above expressions have to be rederived in terms of activities. This exercise is left to the reader.
Below I compare the above three rate laws for the small equilibrium deviation along a constant adsorption isotherm, and for large deviations from equilibrium and isotherm jumping. All rates are computed in terms of activities.
Figure 1 compares the three rates at small equilibrium deviation on the same isotherm. All rates law perform very well. The performance of the small deviation rate law is very good.






Figure 1: Comparison of three rate laws at small deviation from equilibrium on the same isotherm. \(\text{log}_{10}(K_{\text{ex}})\) = 0.2, \(CEC\) = 0.05 mol/kgw, \(k_r\) = 0.1 m/s, \(C^0_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.1 mol/kgw, \(C^0_{\ce{Cl-}}\) = \(C_{\ce{Cl-}}\) = 0.2 mol/kgw, \(C_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.11 mol/kgw. Lithium concentration is obtained from charge balance.



Figure 2 compares the three rates at large equilibrium deviation on the same isotherm. The performance of the small deviation rate law is poor, it under estimates desorption because it essentially decays to a notably different equilibrium state. The other rate laws perform well although are distinct.






Figure 2: Comparison of three rate laws at large deviation from equilibrium on the same isotherm. \(\text{log}_{10}(K_{\text{ex}})\) = 0.2, \(CEC\) = 0.05 mol/kgw, \(k_r\) = 0.1 m/s, \(C^0_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.1 mol/kgw, \(C^0_{\ce{Cl-}}\) = \(C_{\ce{Cl-}}\) = 0.2 mol/kgw, \(C_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.15 mol/kgw. Lithium concentration is obtained from charge balance.



Figure 3 compares the three rates at small jump to a different isotherm. The small deviation rate law is off by a huge margin. It severely over estimates desorption. The other rate laws perform well, and are indistinguishable.






Figure 3: Comparison of three rate laws at small jump to a different isotherm. \(\text{log}_{10}(K_{\text{ex}})\) = 0.2, \(CEC\) = 0.05 mol/kgw, \(k_r\) = 0.1 m/s, \(C^0_{\ce{Na+}}\) = \(C_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.1 mol/kgw, \(C^0_{\ce{Li+}}\) = 1 mol/kgw, \(C_{\ce{Li+}}\) = 0.9 mol/kgw, Chloride concentration is obtained from charge balance.



Figure 4 compares the three rates at large jump to a different isotherm. The performance picture did not change much from the previous example. The small deviation law is off, the isotherm change is catastrophic for its performance. The other rate laws produce the same results. This, however, does not imply they are the same law. They are simply equal at the chosen test conditions.






Figure 4: Comparison of three rate laws at large jump to a different isotherm. \(\text{log}_{10}(K_{\text{ex}})\) = 0.2, \(CEC\) = 0.05 mol/kgw, \(k_r\) = 0.1 m/s, \(C^0_{\ce{Na+}}\) = \(C_{\ce{Na+}}\) = 0.1 mol/kgw, \(C^0_{\ce{Li+}}\) = 1 mol/kgw, \(C_{\ce{Li+}}\) = 0.5 mol/kgw, Chloride concentration is obtained from charge balance.
